{"question_id":"4B.1","answer":"In the 2023 period, Tshisekedi’s government maintained formal electoral competition and held presidential, parliamentary, provincial, and some municipal elections on the constitutional schedule. Candidate registration was politically broad: the Constitutional Court validated 26 presidential candidacies and reinstated two candidates previously excluded by CENI. Diaspora voting, citizen observation, and the planned mixed external voter-register audit were additional formal or procedural safeguards. [BATCH-0028-E010, BATCH-0005-E005, BATCH-0001-E015, BATCH-0023-E015, BATCH-0027-E001, BATCH-0027-E011] Tshisekedi personally instructed state institutions to protect voters and electoral materials, pursue falsification and violence, and uphold non-discrimination, but the supplied evidence does not establish that these instructions were consistently implemented or that he remedied later failures. [BATCH-0009-E001]

The evidence nevertheless does not show power was made reliably or genuinely contestable in practice. Before the election, CENCO-ECC reported conflicting voter totals, duplicated polling stations covering more than two million registered voters, and an omitted territory; CENI’s register was not provided for independent review, and AU/UN audit offers were reportedly declined. [BATCH-0007-E010, BATCH-0013-E009] The CENI’s own account described a mixed international audit that judged the register reliable, but that publication does not independently establish the audit’s independence, findings beyond CENI’s account, or corrective effect. [BATCH-0023-E015, BATCH-0027-E001, BATCH-0027-E011] Public confidence was already weak: only 37 percent of respondents in a January 2023 poll believed CENI could organize credible, free, and transparent elections, although that prospective poll does not prove presidential control or manipulation. [BATCH-0026-E013]

Election-day and counting problems were substantial. Observers reported under-registration, delayed voter-list publication and voter education, inadequate or inaccessible polling infrastructure for older people and persons with disabilities, technical failures, weak ballot-secrecy guarantees, late or closed polling stations, extended voting, procedural deviations, opaque tabulation, and alleged registration or polling irregularities. [BATCH-0001-E013, BATCH-0002-E023, BATCH-0002-E024, BATCH-0001-E016, BATCH-0013-E008, BATCH-0019-E013, BATCH-0028-E011] The Carter Center found the campaign competitive but sometimes unfair because of violence and ruling-coalition administrative-resource abuse; HRW and RSF separately documented attacks or threats involving UDPS supporters and other political actors, restrictions affecting journalists and observers, and authorities’ failure to investigate at least some reported violence. [BATCH-0001-E014, BATCH-0002-E013, BATCH-0002-E014, BATCH-0002-E018, BATCH-0027-E011] Voting did not occur in Rutshuru and Masisi amid armed-group violence, disenfranchising hundreds of thousands, while women initially won 61 of 477 filled National Assembly seats. [BATCH-0013-E011, BATCH-0028-E011]

Tshisekedi was declared and judicially confirmed the winner, and his coalition obtained an overwhelming legislative majority, but opposition candidates disputed the result; CENI later cancelled results in two constituencies and disqualified 82 candidates, including ruling-coalition members. [BATCH-0028-E010, BATCH-0028-E014] His political coordinator urged rival camps to accept the results, but this was not a personal acceptance by Tshisekedi of an adverse result, and no verified opposition victory tested that safeguard. [BATCH-0006-E006] Authorities prohibited an opposition march contesting the election, and police blocked the planned gathering; reported police use of live ammunition remains disputed, though AP journalists observed physical assaults. [BATCH-0021-E009, BATCH-0010-E022]

Overall, the record supports formal electoral pluralism and some ruler-attributed pro-integrity directives, but not a finding that Tshisekedi consistently implemented administration enabling genuinely contestable power. Serious defects in registration, access, campaign conditions, observation, voting, tabulation, and post-election protest materially qualify contestability. Responsibility for most operational failures is institutional, political, conflict-related, or logistical rather than personally proven against Tshisekedi; whether the irregularities changed the presidential result remains
